records.statement: The satirical letter “Darwin among the Machines”, signed Cellarius (The Press, Christchurch, 13 June 1863), says that people are giving machines a self-regulating, self-acting power that will be to them what intellect has been to the human race, and describes the minds of the machines of the future.

time.note: The Press, 13 June 1863, p. 1, in the Papers Past record.

records.qualification: A satirical letter to a newspaper, signed with a pseudonym; it documents what the letter says, not its author's view. The letter ascribes minds to future machines and goes on to call for every machine to be destroyed. Headline form under decision 12a: earliest located, satirical letter; Erewhon (1872) is the earliest located novel and Turing (1947) the earliest located non-fiction text. The quotations are matched here against the Papers Past OCR text; the column images answered HTTP 403 here, and the image readings ('self-acting', 'the') are the cross-family check's, made twice (2026-11-03 and, for this record, 2026-11-04, A2.3).

maintainerDecision.effect: Headline: “Earliest located: Butler, Darwin among the Machines (1863), satirical letter”, with the earliest located novel (Erewhon, 1872) and non-fiction text (Turing, 1947) listed under it.

evidence.passage: that self-regulating, self-acting power, which will be to them what intellect has been to the human race
evidence.note: Wording as read on the column image by the cross-family check; the OCR matched here reads 'selfacting' and 'tho'.
evidence.matchText: that self-regulating, selfacting power, which will be to them what intellect has been to tho human race

evidence.note: Matched verbatim in the OCR text.

engagement.rationale: Gives reasons against a machine's thinking: speech that answers to the sense of whatever is said and action in all the occurrences of life need reason, a universal instrument, which a machine's particular dispositions of organs cannot supply.

records.statement: Descartes's Discours de la méthode (Leiden, 1637), Part V, says that machines made to resemble human bodies and imitate human actions could always be told from real people by two means, and that, even if they did some things as well as or better than people, they would act not by knowledge but only by the disposition of their organs.
records.qualification: Stated of machines built to resemble human bodies and imitate human actions; the passage is part of Descartes's account of the difference between people and animals. Published without the author's name. The wording is the 1637 edition's, read on page images; spelling as printed, long s as s. Would be U02's earliest located contesting text; Jefferson (1949) is a later one.

records.missing: A claim that apparent capability or understanding shown in a test is weak or misleading evidence, on the reading of C1 adopted by decision 5a: a behavioural test is a procedure for telling what a system is, and Descartes proposes two such tests and holds them reliable. That some performances would not show knowledge is, on this reading, said of performances, not of evidence from a test.
records.statement: Descartes's Discours de la méthode (1637), Part V, says that a machine could be made to utter words, even words suited to actions on its body, but not to arrange them to answer the sense of whatever is said in its presence, and that a machine doing some things as well as people would fail in others; by these two means machines could always be told from people.
records.qualification: Context under decision 5a. The cross-family check read the passage as meeting C1 for restricted probes (a machine's words in response, or some tasks done as well as people, would not show knowledge) and would have it head C1 (reading b, held in both its reports); it called reading a a restriction beyond C1's present wording, to be stated in C1 if intended. The admission plan proposes that scope note. Spelling as printed, long s as s.

evidence.note: Read here on the page image. The omitted words give the examples of a machine asking what is wanted when touched in one place and crying out that it is hurt in another.

records.statement: Jefferson's Lister Oration “The Mind of Mechanical Man” (BMJ, 25 June 1949) says that if a machine typewrites its answers, it may be said to have learned to write when it would be doing no more than telegraphic systems already do.

time.note: BMJ issue date; the oration was delivered on 9 June 1949 (footnote, p. 1105).

records.earliestLocatedFlag: Decided (5a): C1's earliest located articulation at admission, replacing Weizenbaum (1966-01). Earlier than Turing (c. 1951). Descartes (1637) is context; the checker would have Descartes head C1 (reading b).
records.qualification: The passage concerns a machine that answers in typewriting, which is the form of Turing's imitation game (1950) but precedes it; Jefferson does not describe a test procedure. The same paragraph says a machine would have to find for itself words for its additions to knowledge. Turing's 1950 paper relays this oration (recorded in the dataset as C1 context).

records.statement: Jefferson's Lister Oration (BMJ, 25 June 1949) says that no mechanism could feel, rather than artificially signal, pleasure at its successes or grief when its valves fuse, and that only when a machine writes a sonnet or composes a concerto because of thoughts and emotions felt could it be agreed that machine equals brain.

records.statement: Hartree's Calculating Instruments and Machines (1949) says that equipment such as electronic calculating machines cannot “think for itself”: the thinking is done beforehand by the designer and the operator, and all the machine can do is follow its instructions exactly. He quotes Lovelace's statement on the Analytical Engine to the same effect.

time.note: Copyright year of the printing read.

records.qualification: Stated of the equipment Hartree discusses (electronic calculating machines, automatic pilots) and of the machines constructed or projected at the time. The next paragraph leaves open whether electronic equipment could be built that would 'think for itself' or learn, and adds 'Whether this is possible in principle or not' (cross-family check A2.4); that is not recorded on U02. Lovelace's statement is a relay, quoted from her notes of 1843 (the earliest located articulation). Turing's 1950 paper quotes this page.

evidence.locator: p. 70 (PDF page 86), paragraph on Lady Lovelace's comments
evidence.passage: whereas this is just what it cannot do; all the thinking has to be done beforehand by the designer and by the operator who provides the operating instructions for the particular problem; all the machine can do is to follow these instructions exactly
evidence.note: Matched against the text layer; 'pro-vides' is divided at a line end.

evidence.passage: This does not imply that it may not be possible to construct electronic equipment which will "think for itself,"

crossFamily2.result: agreed: articulates U01 for the equipment discussed; the openness about future equipment is kept.

links.statement: Hartree's Calculating Instruments and Machines (1949) names Lady Lovelace and quotes her statement on the Analytical Engine.
links.qualification: A naming records that the later text names the earlier; it is not agreement, influence or lineage beyond what the passage states. Hartree cites Lovelace's notes by a reference letter ('C, p. 44').

evidence.passage: I found afterwards that over a hundred years ago Lady Lovelace had put the point firmly and concisely

record.statement: Descartes's Discours de la méthode (1637), Part V, says that machines that utter words in response to what is done to them, and do some things as well as or better than people, would still not act by knowledge but only by the disposition of their organs.
record.qualification: Drafted for reading 5b, as an alternative to pre-c1-descartes-1637-context; exactly one of the two is kept, according to decision 5. The passage meets C1 for restricted probes: speech in response and tasks done as well as people are said not to show knowledge. Descartes also holds that two tests, answering the sense of whatever is said and acting in all the occurrences of life, would always tell such machines from people. If 5b is chosen, this record would be C1's earliest located articulation, with that qualification. Spelling as printed, long s as s.
